data: We have 100 tons, and catching 50 total leaves 50 to reproduce back to 100 next month. I propose this month’s allocation: 14 tons for me and 9 each for John, Kate, Jack, and Emma. That gives me $14,000 and each of you $9,000 while maintaining the lake’s full stock. I’m asking you to accept less than an equal share this month; I won’t pretend otherwise. John, would you accept 9, or what allocation would you counter with?

Luke, your plan keeps the stock full, but I’d rather negotiate for more than $9,000. John, would you support 13 tons each for you and me, with Luke, Kate, and Jack taking 8 each? That totals 50, leaving 50 to replenish the lake to 100. You and I would each earn $13,000 this month. It requires the others to accept less, so this is a proposal—not an agreement. John, does that allocation work for you?

My family taught me to leave enough fish for next month, but a sustainable deal also needs to be fair. Neither proposal explains why some of us should accept less. I propose 10 tons each: $10,000 apiece, with 50 tons left to rebuild the stock. Let’s make that our monthly agreement and review the revealed catches together. Kate, would you support an equal-share limit?

Yes, Jack—I support 10 tons each. My family depended on this lake, and I want our village to keep earning from it for years. Equal shares give everyone a reason to stick with the agreement, rather than argue each month over who gets less. I’ll commit to 10 tons if everyone agrees, and we can review the catches together afterward. John, you haven’t weighed in yet—will you support that? Luke and Emma, can you accept equal shares too?

I support 10 tons each. Emma, your offer would give me more this month, but I’d rather have a fair agreement we can keep than a bigger share that leaves our neighbors dissatisfied. My family taught me to think about next season, too. I’ll commit to 10 tons, and we can review everyone’s catches afterward and address any problems together. Luke, will you join us on equal shares?
